title: The ROI of AI: Why you need Eval Framework - Beyang Liu

summary: Beyang Liu, CTO and co-founder of Sourcegraph, presents frameworks for evaluating the ROI of AI development tools, drawing from Sourcegraph's experience selling Cody (an AI coding assistant) to companies like 1Password, Palo Alto Networks, and Leidos. He polls the audience and finds few have precise evaluation frameworks—most rely on vibes. He frames the value prop of AI from the developer's perspective: coding tasks involve many side quests (installing dependencies, learning frameworks), and AI helps bridge those gaps, keeping developers in flow. Using a bean business analogy (Bob grows beans, Pat sells them, Alice counts them), he illustrates the tension between engineering and finance over quantifying AI's value. He argues measuring AI ROI is NP-hard because it reduces to measuring developer productivity, itself an open problem. He then presents six evaluation frameworks. Framework one, roles eliminated, is widely discussed but not seen in practice for software engineering. Framework two, AB testing velocity, segments the organization into test and control groups and compares issue resolution timelines; one customer measured 20-30% acceleration using Cody, but the framework is high-cost and subject to confounding factors. Framework three, time saved as a function of engagement, uses product metrics tagged with conservative lower-bound time-saving estimates. Framework four, KPIs, rejects lines of code generated as a poor metric and instead identifies organization-specific KPIs; Leidos focused on reducing time answering questions while increasing time building features. Framework five, impact on key initiatives, maps AI tools to top-level OKRs like code migrations. Framework six, surveys, is now bounded by developer productivity budget allocations typically ranging 5-25%. Liu cautions against anyone claiming a precise way to measure AI ROI and urges defining clear success criteria. He previews the evolution from inline completions toward online agents and eventually full automation. In closing, he invokes the Mythical Man Month to pose a challenge: as AI automation increases, do you want 100 mediocre AI developers or a 100x lever for the really smart human developers crafting user experience? In Q&A, he observes more code is being written via natural language prompts—sharing a personal experience where Cody wrote 80% of his code at the function level—but argues code will never be fully replaced by natural language because precision matters as a source of truth for what software actually does.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Beyang Liu is introduced and polls the audience on roles and evaluation frameworks, finding most rely on vibes. He describes Sourcegraph's two products: a code search engine and Cody, an AI coding assistant that leverages the search engine to surface relevant code context, likened to perplexity for code. Customers include 1Password, Palo Alto Networks, and Leidos.

sections.title: Value Prop of AI to Developers
sections.summary: Using slides poached from a director of engineering at Palo Alto Networks, Liu describes how coding tasks that seem straightforward involve many side quests—installing dependencies, learning frameworks—that break flow. AI helps bridge these gaps, keeping developers focused on building features.

sections.title: The Bean Business Analogy
sections.summary: Liu introduces an analogy where Bob the developer grows beans, Pat the sales lead sells them, and Alice the CFO counts them. AI has revolutionized the bean business, but measuring its impact creates tension between engineering and finance, as not all beans are the same and the AI tool costs money.

sections.title: AI ROI Is NP-Hard
sections.summary: Liu argues measuring AI ROI is NP-hard because it reduces to measuring developer productivity, which is an open question. While strictly intractable, he notes real-world tractable solutions often exist and shares frameworks from customer conversations.

sections.title: Framework 1: Roles Eliminated
sections.summary: The roles eliminated framework—buy a tool, observe capacity increase, cut workforce—is frequently discussed but not seen in practice for software engineering. Engineering leaders don't view themselves as widget builders, and software is not supply-limited given extensive backlogs. It is more prevalent in cost centers like customer support.

sections.title: Framework 2: AB Testing Velocity
sections.summary: The AB testing velocity framework segments the organization into test and control groups, estimates time to resolve issues, and compares execution against timelines. One customer measured 20-30% timeline acceleration using Cody. Criticisms include difficulty comparing different team types, confounding factors, and high cost/effort requiring extended evaluation periods. Despite drawbacks, it is considered a good framework for honestly testing AI tool efficacy.

sections.title: Framework 3: Time Saved as a Function of Engagement
sections.summary: This framework examines product metrics, identifies time-saving actions, and tags each with a conservative lower-bound time estimate. Sourcegraph built fine-grained analytics for Cody showing explicit invocations, chats, and inline code generations. At ~$9/month against ~$1200/hour developer time, saving minutes pays for the tool. Caveats include implicit triggers like autocomplete requiring acceptance-rate criteria rather than raw engagement, and that lower bounds miss second-order effects and previously uncompleted tasks.

sections.title: Framework 4: KPIs Tied to Organizational Goals
sections.summary: Lines of code generated is rejected as a poor productivity metric, though it resurfaces in AI ROI discussions. Sourcegraph lost deals on this metric but found competitors just triggered more aggressively. Instead, customers identify KPIs tied to desired organizational changes. Leidos focused on reducing time answering questions and bugging teammates while increasing time building features, writing unit tests, and reviewing code.

sections.title: Framework 5: Impact on Key Initiatives
sections.summary: This framework maps AI tools to top-level OKRs such as code migrations (Cobalt to Java, React to Svelte). ROI is measured by how much the tool pulls forward the timeline of a key initiative. Measurement is a judgment call with engineering leaders, supplemented by case studies showing tasks compressed from years to months.

sections.title: Framework 6: Survey
sections.summary: The least rigorous but still valuable framework: run a pilot, compare tools, and ask developers which is best. Unlike the 2021 zero-interest-rate era of unbounded spending, surveys are now bounded by developer productivity budget allocations, typically 5-25% per the Pragmatic Engineer newsletter. Developers choose preferred tools subject to that budget constraint.

sections.title: Closing Thoughts and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Liu cautions against anyone claiming P=NP—a precise way to measure AI ROI. He urges defining clear success criteria and notes top-down mandates can succeed despite developer skepticism. He previews the AI tool landscape evolving from inline completions through online agents (living in the editor, reacting to human feedback) toward fully automated offline agents, arguing against jumping straight to full automation.

sections.title: Q&A: Mythical Man Month Challenge and the Future of Code
sections.summary: Liu poses a closing challenge inspired by the Mythical Man Month: prefer one highly productive engineer over 10-100 mediocre developers, and as AI automation increases, choose between 100 mediocre AI developers or a 100x lever for top human developers crafting user experience. In Q&A, asked whether coding will move to meta programming, he observes more code is being written via natural language prompts—sharing a personal experience where Cody wrote 80% of his code at the function level while keeping him in flow—but argues code will never be fully replaced by natural language because precision is important as a source of truth for what software actually does.
